source_text: Eadem igitur forma, caetera quoque ad martyrii pertinere defendimus. Qui pluris, inquit, fecerit etiam animam suam quam me, non est me dignus; id est, qui maluerit vivere me negando, quam mori confitendo. Qui animam suam invenerit, perdet illam; qui vero perdiderit mei caussa, inveniet illam. Proinde enim invenit eam, qui negarit lucrifaciendo vitam; sed perdet in gehennam, qui se putat negando lucrifacere eam. Perdet autem eam ad praesens, qui confessus occiditur; sed inventurus eam in vitam aeternam. Ipsi denique praesides, cum hortantur negationi, serva animam tuam, dicunt, et noli animam tuam perdere. Quo modo loqueretur Christus, nisi quo modo tractaretur christianus? Sed cum prohibet meditari responsionem ad tribunal, famulos suos instruit, Spiritum Sanctum responsurum repromittit; et cum in carcere fratrem vult visitari, confessoris imperat curam; et cum Deum vindictam facturum electorum suorum affirmat, passiones consolatur illorum: etiam in parabola seminis post cespitem arefacti, persecutionum figurat ardorem. Haec si non ita accipiuntur quemadmodum pronuntiantur, sine dubio praeterquam sonant sapiunt; et aliud in vocibus erit, aliud in sensibus; ut allegoriae, ut parabolae, ut aenigmata. Quemcumque igitur conceperint ventum argumentationis scorpii isti, quocumque se acumine impegerint, una jam linea est: ad ipsas res provocabuntur, an secundum Scripturas transigantur. Siquidem tunc aliud significabitur in Scripturis, si non idipsum reperiatur in rebus. Quod enim scriptum est, hoc evenire oportebit. Porro, tunc eveniet quod est scriptum, si non aliud eveniet. Ecce autem et odio habemur ab omnibus hominibus, nominis caussa, quomodo et scriptum est; et tradimur etiam a proximis, quomodo et scriptum est; et perducimur ad potestates, et interrogamur, et torquemur, et confitemur, et trucidamur, quomodo et scriptum est. Sic Dominus edixit. Si aliter edixit haec, cur non aliter eveniunt, quam edixit, id est, quemadmodum edixit? Atquin non aliter eveniunt quam edixit: ergo sicut eveniunt, ita edixit, ita eveniunt. Nam nec licuisset aliter evenire, quam edixit; nec ipse aliter edixisset, quam evenire voluisset. Ita, non aliud significabunt Scripturae, quam in rebus recognoscimus. Aut si nondum aguntur illa quae praedicantur, quomodo haec aguntur quae praedicata non sunt? Non sunt enim haec praedicata quae aguntur, si alia sunt quae praedicantur, et non haec quae aguntur. At nunc, quia ipsa sunt in rebus, quae in vocibus, aliter dicta creduntur; quid fieret si aliter facta invenirentur? Sed haec est perversitas fidei, probata non credere, non probata praesumere. Cui perversitati illud quoque opponam, ut si haec quae sic aguntur quemadmodum scripta sunt, non erunt ipsa quae praedicantur, illa quae non debeant sic agi quemadmodum scripta sunt, ne et ipsa horum exemplo periclitentur, excludi siquidem aliud in vocibus, aliud in rebus est; et relinquitur nec praedicata videri cum evenerint, si aliter praedicantur quam evenire habent. Et quomodo credentur quae non erunt praedicata, quia non ita erunt praedicata quomodo eveniunt? Ita haeretici quae praedicantur non ut probata sunt credendo, ea quae nec praedicata sunt, credunt.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, we defend that the same form also pertains to the rest of martyrdom. He who does more, he says, and also considers his soul more than me, is not worthy of me; that is, he who prefers to live by denying me rather than to die by confessing. He who finds his soul will lose it; but he who loses it for my sake will find it. For he finds it, who denies it by gaining life; but he loses it in Gehenna, who thinks he gains it by denying. But he loses it now, who is killed after confessing; yet he will find it in eternal life. Even the judges themselves, when they encourage denial, say: Save your soul, and do not lose your soul. How would Christ speak, if not in the way a Christian is treated? But when he forbids meditating on a response to the tribunal, he instructs his servants, and promises that the Holy Spirit will respond; and when he wants a brother in prison to be visited, he commands care for the confessor; and when he affirms that God will avenge his elect, he consoles their passions: and also in the parable of the seed after the thorns have been dried up, he figures the ardor of persecutions. If these things are not accepted as they are pronounced, they undoubtedly sound different from what they mean; and there will be one thing in words, another in meanings; like allegories, like parables, like riddles. Whichever argument these scorpions conceive, with whatever sharpness they attack, there is now one line: they will be provoked to the things themselves, whether they are transacted according to the Scriptures. For if then something else is signified in the Scriptures, if the same thing is not found in the things, what is written will not happen. But then what is written will happen, if something else does not happen. Behold, we are hated by all men, for the sake of the name, as it is written; and we are betrayed even by our neighbors, as it is written; and we are led to the authorities, and questioned, and tortured, and confess, and are slaughtered, as it is written. So the Lord decreed. If he decreed these things otherwise, why do they not happen otherwise, than he decreed, that is, as he decreed? But they do not happen otherwise than he decreed: therefore, as they happen, so he decreed, so they happen. For it was not permitted for them to happen otherwise, than he decreed; nor would he have decreed otherwise, than he wanted to happen. So, the Scriptures will not signify anything else, than what we recognize in the things. Or if those things which are predicted are not yet done, how are these things done which are not predicted? For these things which are done are not predicted, if other things are predicted, and not these things which are done. But now, because the same things are in the things, which are in the words, they are believed to have been said otherwise; what would happen if they were found to have been done otherwise? But this is the perversity of faith, not to believe what is proven, to presume what is not proven. To this perversity I will also oppose this, that if these things which are done in this way, as they are written, are not the same things which are predicted, those things which ought not to be done in this way, as they are written, will also be endangered by the example of these; for if something else is excluded in words, something else in things, it remains that what is predicted is not seen when it happens, if it is predicted otherwise than it will happen. And how will those things be believed which are not predicted, because they are not predicted in this way, as they happen? So heretics do not believe what is predicted, as it has been proven by believing, but they believe what is not predicted.

pass_b_english: We argue that the same pattern governs the rest of martyrdom. "Whoever values even his own life above me is not worthy of me" (Matt. 10:37) -- that is, whoever chooses to live by denying me rather than die by confessing me. "Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matt. 10:39). The denier thinks he has saved his life by gaining the present world, but he actually loses it in Gehenna. The confessor loses his life now by execution, yet will recover it in eternal life. Even the magistrates, when they urge apostasy, parrot the same logic: "Save your life; don't throw it away." How else would Christ speak than through the treatment his followers receive? When he forbids rehearsing a defense before the court, he is coaching his servants and promising the Holy Spirit will supply the answer (Matt. 10:19-20). When he asks that a brother in prison be visited, he is commanding care for the confessor (Matt. 25:36). When he declares God will avenge his elect, he is comforting their sufferings (Luke 18:7-8). Even in the parable of the seed scorched after the thorns wither, he maps the heat of persecution (Matt. 13:5-6, 20-21).

If these words are not taken exactly as they are spoken, they merely sound different from what they mean -- words and sense split apart like allegories, parables, riddles. Let the scorpion-arguers conceive whatever wind of argument they like, let them strike with whatever sting: the issue has narrowed to a single line -- will the facts themselves be forced to conform to Scripture? Because if Scripture ends up signifying something other than what actually occurs, then what is written will not happen. But what is written will happen only if nothing else happens instead. Look: we are hated by all for the Name, just as it is written (Matt. 10:22); betrayed by our own kin, just as it is written (Matt. 10:21); dragged before authorities, interrogated, tortured, confessing, and slaughtered, just as it is written (Matt. 24:9). The Lord decreed it so. If he had decreed otherwise, why do events not unfold otherwise -- that is, as he decreed? But they do not unfold otherwise; therefore, as they happen, so he decreed, and so they happen. It was never permitted for them to happen differently than he decreed, nor would he have decreed differently than he willed them to happen.

Thus Scripture signifies nothing other than what we recognize in the facts. Or if the predicted events have not yet occurred, how are these unpredicted events occurring? The events happening now are not the predicted ones if the predicted ones are different. But now, because the facts match the words, people believe the words meant something else; what would happen if the facts turned out differently? This is faith's perversity: refusing to believe what is proven, presuming what is not. To that perversity I add this: if the events happening exactly as written are not the predicted events, then the events that should not happen as written are also endangered by this precedent. For if words and facts are divorced, the predicted events will not be recognized when they arrive, since they were predicted differently than they occur. And how will anyone believe events that were not predicted, simply because they were not predicted in the way they happen? That is how heretics operate: they disbelieve what was predicted and proven, and believe what was never predicted at all.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical structure of Tertullian's argument regarding the correspondence between Scripture and reality. Pass A provides a faithful literal translation of the Latin, while Pass B provides a more readable version that correctly incorporates the required inline scripture citations (e.g., Matt. 10:37, Matt. 10:39, Matt. 10:22, etc.) which correspond to the Latin text's allusions. The distinction between 'words' (vocibus) and 'things/facts' (rebus) is maintained throughout.
